info.bio:
James Newell Osterberg, Jr., más conocido por su nombre artístico, Iggy Pop, nació en Muskegon, Michigan el 21 de abril de 1947. Es un cantante estadounidense de punk rock. Pese a tener un éxito comercial limitado es considerado uno de los mayores innovadores en el punk rock y estilos relacionados.

Iggy fue el cantante de The Stooges una banda de fines de los 60 y principio de los 70 muy influyente en desarrollo del punk. The Stooges se hizo famosa por sus actuaciones en vivo

scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y sus herederos
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: La línea de art rock que reivindica el postpunk no es la del progresivo sinfónico sino la que va de The Velvet Underground al krautrock y al glam intelectual, fiel al principio minimalista «menos es más». Durante el «páramo» de los setenta, un racimo de espíritus afines unidos por su deuda con la Velvet (Lou Reed, John Cale, Nico, Iggy Pop, Bowie, Eno) colaboró en distintas combinaciones y sostuvo a los hipsters.

scenes.name: Bowie e Iggy en Berlín
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Más que Never Mind the Bollocks o el debut de The Clash, al postpunk lo marcaron los cuatro discos de Bowie de 1977: Low y Heroes, y The Idiot y Lust for Life de Iggy Pop. Grabados en Berlín, se alejan de Estados Unidos y del rock'n'roll hacia un sonido europeo, frío y controlado, sobre los ritmos motorik de Kraftwerk y Neu!, con los sintetizadores al mismo nivel que las guitarras. El lado dos de Low, con Brian Eno («texturólogo supremo»), es una suite de atmósferas crepusculares. Eno se convierte después en uno de los productores que definen la era (no wave, Devo, Talking Heads, U2).

scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.

podcast.body: Iggy Pop began making music in 1965, marking an early start in the business, though not the longest-running as identified by the record. His career began a year after David Bowie's first record. "He started making music in 1965."

podcast.title: Accidental Guitar Incident and Stage Persona Birth (October 30-31, 1967)
podcast.body: The day before The Stooges' first show, guitarist Ron Ashton painted Iggy's Hawaiian guitar, including the pickups, rendering it useless. Iggy took the guitar on stage anyway, then abandoned it, dancing "like a nut" as his pants began to fall down. When the audience reacted positively, believing it was part of the show, Iggy amplified his erratic behavior, which was the foundational moment for his punk rock stage persona. "And it was this event that set Iggy on the road to becoming the Godfather of Punk."

podcast.body: In 1967, Iggy Pop was profoundly influenced by seeing The Doors perform in Detroit, marveling at Jim Morrison's provocative stage presence and confrontational style, which made him think he could push boundaries even further. "He couldn't believe how provocative Jim Morrison was."

podcast.title: Financial Mismanagement and Eccentric Behavior (1969-1973)
podcast.body: During the period of The Stooges' three major label albums, Iggy Pop was "totally off the deep end," spending $100,000 of his record company advance on a suite at a Beverly Hills hotel. He developed a substantial "coconut hair one habit" and was arrested multiple times, including for impersonating a female (which was a crime then), and once took an axe to a wealthy one-night stand's Mercedes. "He spent $100,000 of his record company advance on a suite at a Beverly Hills hotel. He had a huge coconut hair one habit that needed to be fed."

podcast.title: Elton John Gorilla Incident (1973)
podcast.body: In October 1973, while the Stooges were on a punishing tour and Iggy was heavily incapacitated by Quaaludes, Elton John—dressed in a rented gorilla suit—surprised Iggy on stage at Richard's Club in Atlanta as part of a prank and a potential move to sign the band. Iggy, hallucinating, freaked out believing it was a real gorilla, and the band's guitarist James Williamson almost attacked Elton before his identity was revealed. "Elton John dressed in a gorilla suit, bounds on stage. Iggy, in his altered state and seeing triple, freaked out, thinking that this was a real gorilla."

podcast.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
podcast.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."

podcast.title: Confrontation at Michigan Palace (1974)
podcast.body: Following a brutal confrontation with a Detroit gang, Iggy Pop performed at Michigan Palace where he provocatively demanded that the gang come on stage and "beat him to a pulp," with some friends believing he sought to die on stage. The audience responded by throwing beer bottles, not all of them empty, at the stage, an incident captured on the album "Metallic KO." "Years later a cassette recording of that performance would be released on an album called Metallic KO."

He had no money or place to live, and the low point came when the LAPD found him hiding under the counter of a burger joint. "In 1974, his band, the stooge's head, broken up and Iggy was reduced to a babbling, wandering junkie prone to blockouts."

podcast.title: Regeneration in West Berlin (May 1976)
podcast.body: In late May 1976, Iggy Pop moved to West Berlin with David Bowie to escape their destructive lifestyles in Los Angeles and to regenerate among the city's diverse community of bohemians, weirdos, drug addicts, prostitutes, and transsexuals. This move, prompted by Bowie's heart attack scare in the fall of 1976, led both artists to seriously clean up their acts and embark on an incredibly creative period. "So in late May 1976, Bowie and Iggy moved to West Berlin to regenerate in the company of the Bohemians and weirdos and drug addicts and prostitutes and transsexuals who lived there."

xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.body: Living in Los Angeles had severely impacted David Bowie's sanity, leaving him in a fog of alcohol and cocaine abuse. He developed severe paranoia, believing aliens were coming to collect him, and reportedly collected his urine in jars as protection against alien abduction. Recognizing the need for a change, Bowie moved to West Berlin in late May 1976 with Iggy Pop to detoxify and regenerate amidst the city's bohemian and unconventional inhabitants. "Living in LA had seriously jeopardized their sanity."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 1980)
xref.body: Ian Curtis died by suicide on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures exacerbated by a "crazy cocktail" of prescriptions, drinking, illegal drug use, poor diet, and late nights. He also faced an impending divorce, an affair with a Belgian woman, money worries, and pressure to continue performing with Joy Division despite his problems. The final Joy Division show on May 2, 1980, saw Ian faint during the last song, experiencing another grand mal seizure, leading to the cancellation of their upcoming North American tour. On the evening of May 17, Ian returned to his home at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife Deborah was out. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on May 18, he put on his favorite album, "The Idiot" by Iggy Pop, went to the garden for a length of rope from the clothesline, and hanged himself. Deborah found him a few hours later. "He'd been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures that were exacerbated by a crazy cocktail of prescriptions, drinking illegal drug use, poor diet late nights, an impending divorce, and a ferry was having with a woman from Belgium worries about money and pressures to keep on performing with the band despite all these problems."

xref.title: Final Hours and Suicide (1980)
xref.body: On the evening of May 17th, Ian returned to his house at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife, Deborah, was working as a bartender at a wedding reception. They spoke, and Ian requested time alone, with Deborah agreeing not to return until after 10 AM the next morning, spending the night at her parents' house. After she left, Ian watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank several cups of strong coffee and a shot of whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on Sunday, May 18th, he put on Iggy Pop's "The Idiot," retrieved a rope from his garden's clothesline, and hanged himself. "Once she was gone, Ian sat down to watch his movie, which was a 1977 film entitled Strozek, which follows a musician and form a mental patient who travels to the US and is unable to decide between the two women in his life."

xref.title: Admiration by British Punks
xref.body: The early British punks loved Bowie, admiring his concise songs, bold fashion, and rebellious attitude of not caring what others thought, even in the face of ridicule. His friendships with "cool" figures like Iggy Pop and Lou Reed, and his willingness to "kill himself off" creatively, also resonated deeply with them. "The kids who would become the first generation of British punks loved Bowie. They admired the short, sharp songs, his wild fashion sense, and the way he acted like he didn't care about what anybody thought."

xref.title: Confrontational Stage Presence & Stage Diving
xref.body: The Stooges developed a divisive live reputation, attracting audiences who either loved or hated them. xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

xref.body: Despite being dismissed by many for their unconventional style, the New York Dolls developed a significant following among those who appreciated "weird things." They were seen by some as embodying the true spirit of rock and roll, where attitude and energy surpassed virtuosity. The band regularly played alongside other influential artists like Iggy Pop and KISS. "People like Iggy Pop and Lou Reed and The New York Dolls... in retrospect, these are incredibly important people to our story."

xref.title: Educator and Champion of Obscure Artists
xref.body: Through his collaborations with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed, and his early championing of The Velvet Underground, Bowie acted as an educator in music, helping to spread awareness and appreciation for these otherwise obscure performers. "Through his work with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed, and through his early championing of the Velvet Underground, Bowie acted as an educator, a person who helped spread the word on these otherwise obscure performers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 2

xref.title: Extreme Behavior and Drug Use
xref.body: The Stooges were known for their wild and intense performances, with Iggy Pop being particularly unhinged. The band extensively used drugs, including heroin and Angel Dust, leading to self-destructive behavior and an out-of-control reputation. "They were on every drug known to man all the way up to heroin and Angel Dust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

xref.title: Extreme Contrast to Mainstream and Hippie Bands
xref.body: The Stooges, particularly through Iggy Pop's antics, presented a "crazy" and extreme alternative that starkly contrasted with mainstream acts like The Beatles and The Rolling Stones, and was also distinct from the prevailing hippie groups. "This wasn't anything mainstream bands like the beetles or the stones we're doing. And the hippie groups, certainly weren't into this kind of thing either."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

xref.title: Extreme Performances
xref.body: The Stooges, featuring Iggy Pop, were known for their "extreme things" performed in America, contributing to the outrageous aesthetic that inspired David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona. "who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Failed Attempt to Sign The Stooges
xref.body: Despite his dramatic stage appearance in a gorilla suit, Elton John's mutual admiration with Iggy Pop and The Stooges did not result in him signing the band to a record contract. "Elton never did sign him or the band to a record contract."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1

xref.title: Fascination with The Stooges
xref.body: David Bowie found The Stooges, particularly Iggy Pop, "profoundly fascinating," which later led to their collaboration. "David Bowie found them profoundly fascinating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Featured in Punk Magazine
xref.body: The fanzine "Punk," which appeared at the end of 1975, covered The New York Dolls, among other raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s and artists in the burgeoning CBGB scene. "It also covered Iggy Pop and the Stooges, The New York Dolls, and even some of their raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s like Question Mark and Mysterians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Breakup and Iggy's Hiatus
xref.body: Eventually, the band dissolved. Iggy Pop spent the next six months in Florida cutting lawns for retirees. "Eventually, the stuages were done. Iggy spent the next six months in Florida cutting lawns for retirees."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Show (Halloween, Year Not Specified)
xref.body: Iggy Pop formed The Psychedelic Stooges in the summer of 1967, and their first show was a private party held on Halloween. The performance was reportedly so poor that their manager quit and returned to his job as a school teacher. "they played their first show at a private party that Halloween. It wasn't very good, so bad that their manager quit and went back to his job as a school teacher."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

xref.title: First to Crossover to Mainstream
xref.body: R.E.M. is recognized as one of the first and largest bands from the college/alternative rock scene to successfully cross over into mainstream consciousness. Their success helped popularize "alternative" as an umbrella term for distinct rock music. "I guess REM was the first and the biggest, the word alternative became more widely used as this umbrella term for rock music that was different that did not descend from the Beatles and the Stones and Led Zeppelin, but from Bowie and Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground and the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 8

xref.title: Formation and Influence – Post-Drumming for Iggy Pop
xref.body: After his initial drumming experiences, Iggy Pop moved on from behind the drum kit to start writing songs and formed The Stooges. This band, along with Iggy's subsequent involvement with David Bowie and other experiences, contributed significantly to laying the foundations for modern punk rock. "He started writing songs moved on to the stooges got involved with David Bowie took a lot of LSD and pretty much laid the foundations for modern punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Drummers

xref.title: Glam Rock Inspirations
xref.body: Bowie's full dive into Glam Rock was inspired by Mark Bolan, his "crazy new friend" Iggy Pop, another friend Lou Reed, and a 1968 seven-inch single called "Paralyzed" by "The Legendary Stardust Cowboy." Drawing on his background as an actor and mime, Bowie meticulously experimented with makeup and costuming. "Inspired by Bowen, his crazy new friend Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, another new friend, and a seven inch single from 1968 called Paralyzed by a guy calling himself the legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie went all in."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 1

xref.title: Glam Rock Transformation - Haircut and Fashion
xref.body: Inspired by Marc Bolan, Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, and The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, Bowie went "all in" on glam rock. A key element was his haircut, replicated and modified from a model in a magazine wearing Kansai Yamamoto clothes, razor-cut at the sides and back, backcombed into a "puffy fluff ball," and dyed reddish-orange at Yamamoto's suggestion. This, combined with makeup and costuming, transformed him into the "elfin cute boy in the dress" to something "never before seen in music." "Bowie fun to picture of a model in a magazine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1

xref.title: Godfather of Grunge
xref.body: Neil Young is recognized as the "godfather of Grunge," particularly in Seattle where he was a big favorite. His career phase in the 1970s, characterized by "obnoxiously overdriven guitar grinding under a simple melody" and a "calculated sloppiness," held a specific appeal that deeply resonated with and influenced the burgeoning Seattle music scene. "If Iggy Pop was the godfather of punk, the Ramones, with the Johnny Apples seeds of alt rock, well then Neil Young, a big favorite in Seattle, is the godfather of Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 11

xref.title: Hansa Studio 2 - Berlin
xref.body: Bowie and Iggy Pop made music seriously at Hansa Studio 2 in Berlin, located approximately 100 meters from the Berlin Wall, a place where Bowie produced Iggy's album "The Idiot" and recorded two of his own albums. "Berlin also had a very good recording studio called Hansa, all of 100-ish meters from where the Berlin wall ran through the city."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2

xref.title: Hit Version of China Girl
xref.body: David Bowie released his own recording of "China Girl," a song he co-wrote with Iggy Pop in 1977, in the early 1980s. His version became a big hit, generating significant royalties (close to a million dollars) for Iggy Pop. "A song co-written by David Bowie who of course had a big hit with his own recording of that song in the early 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Iggy Pop's Beating and Challenge
xref.body: While the rest of the band fled, Iggy Pop remained to confront the bikers, jumping into the crowd and receiving a severe beating before being dragged out, possibly saving his life. Days later, Iggy appeared on the radio, promoting an upcoming show and boldly challenging the Scorpions to a rematch. "He stayed there to confront the bikers, jumping into the crowd. And he got a pretty good beating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

xref.title: Iggy Pop's Name Origin
xref.body: James Newell Osterberg adopted the stage name "Iggy" from his previous band, The Iguanas. The "Pop" part was added after he shaved off his eyebrows in a "weird stoned gesture," leading the other band members to comment that he resembled a local drug user named Jim Pop. "The pop part came after Iggy shaved off his eyebrows in some weird stone to gesture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Iggy Pop's Stage Antics
xref.body: Iggy Pop was notorious for scaring audiences with his antics, which included smearing peanut butter on himself and carving his body with broken glass from bottles thrown at him on stage. "He'd smear peanut butter all over himself and often carve himself up with broken glass from the beer bottles that were thrown at him on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

xref.title: Iggy Pop's Unusual Stage Attire
xref.body: During their first public performance, Iggy Pop appeared on stage wearing a nightshirt, golf shoes, white mime makeup, and a large afro wig made from tinfoil. "Iggy was wearing a night shirt and golf shoes and white mime makeup and a big afro wig made out of tinfoil."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

xref.title: Iggy's Survival and Drug Dealing (Early 1970s)
xref.body: During the band's inactive period after being dropped by Elektra, Iggy Pop sustained himself by becoming a middleman for a heroin dealer. However, he often used the drugs himself, exacerbating his addiction. "Iggy paid the bills by becoming a middleman for a hairwind dealer, but sometimes he forgot his role and ended up using all the drugs himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Implied Soviet Blacklist - Violence
xref.body: Though listed as "The Stages" on the USSR's 1985 "not recommended music" list, it is speculated that Soviet authorities were likely referring to Iggy Pop and The Stooges when they cited "Violence" as a reason for prohibition. This indicates the perceived aggressive or disruptive influence of their music. "The Stages, I think they meant Iggy Pop and the Stooges, Violence, ACDC, Neo-Fascism and Violence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy

xref.title: Influence of Iggy Pop
xref.body: Bowie incorporated elements from the "outrageous behavior" of his friend Iggy Pop, who performed extreme acts with his band The Stooges in America, into the Ziggy Stardust persona. "borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop, who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on "Punk" Terminology
xref.body: Lester Banks, a Detroit rock writer, extensively covered the kind of rock performed by The Stooges and Iggy Pop. His writings helped to shape the early critical understanding of this raw and energetic style of music, which was later associated with the "punk" aesthetic. "Lester Banks began spewing out thousands and thousands of rapturous words on the kind of rock played by the Count Five, Iggy Pop and the Stooges and others of their ilk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

xref.title: Influence on Alt-Rock Icons
xref.body: Despite his humble beginnings with The Shades, Lou Reed later became a foundational influence on many significant artists in the alt-rock scene. His work inspired figures such as David Bowie, Iggy Pop, R.E.M., and The Killers. "he would later influence Bowie and Iggy and R.E.M. and the killers and so many of the other movers and shakers of the alt-rock scene in the decades ahead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

xref.title: Influence on Bowie and Punk
xref.body: Lou Reed was a new friend who inspired David Bowie's glam rock experimentation. His past membership in The Velvet Underground, coupled with his friendship with Bowie, also made Bowie "cool" in the eyes of the early British punks. "Inspired by Bowlin, his crazy new friend Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, another new friend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1

xref.title: Influence on British Punk - Sex Pistols Connection
xref.body: Bowie's "outsider-ness," short, sharp songs, wild fashion sense, and defiant attitude endeared him to alienated working-class youth who would become the first generation of British punks. His friendships with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed (of The Velvet Underground) also made him "cool" in their eyes. Famously, on July 2nd, 1973, after Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon, a young Steve Jones (later guitarist for the Sex Pistols) stole microphones and amps from the venue, gear that would be used to start his new band. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1

xref.title: Influence on Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine
xref.body: The Velvet Underground were among the influential artists from the underground music scene on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" that deeply resonated with Legs McNeill. His appreciation for such bands ultimately led him to establish the "Punk" fanzine, documenting this emerging musical culture. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Lou Reed was a pivotal figure on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" underground music scene whose work Legs McNeill greatly admired. McNeill included Reed among the artists he celebrated and featured in his influential "Punk" fanzine, contributing to the definition of the burgeoning punk aesthetic. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

xref.body: Patti Smith was an artist from the underground music scene on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" who inspired Legs McNeill. Her work, along with that of others, was part of the musical landscape that McNeill loved and documented in his seminal "Punk" fanzine. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

xref.title: Influenced Major Artists
xref.body: The Velvet Underground is credited with awakening and influencing a wide array of prominent artists and bands, including David Bowie, Roxy Music, The Doors, Patti Smith, Iggy Pop and the Stooges, U2, Joy Division, The Pixies, The Sex Pistols, Talking Heads, The Cure, Kraftwerk, R.E.M., Simple Minds, The Strokes, and The Psychedelic Furs, whose name derived from a Velvet Underground song. "Here is a list of just some of the few who claimed to have been awakened by the velvet underground and then incorporated some of whatever they were doing into their music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Norman O'Dan, a Texas proto-psychobilly singer also known as The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, was a big fan of space travel and admired by David Bowie. He was one of the two people who inspired the name for Bowie's alien rock star character, Ziggy, in *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*. "And that name was inspired by two people, Bowie's new friend Iggy Pop, and a Texas proto-psychobilly singer named Norman O'Dan, who went by the handle of the legendary Stardust Cowboy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Concept Albums: Part 1

xref.title: Inspiration for Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: David Bowie's iconic Ziggy Stardust character was partly inspired by the American singer Vince Taylor, known for his 1959 song "Brand New Cadillac." "The original was by Vince Taylor, an American singer who provided part of the inspiration for David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: James Williamson's Career Shift
xref.body: Following the initial breakup, guitarist James Williamson had a brief reunion with Iggy Pop in 1979 but then retired from music to become an electronics engineer. He earned an electrical engineering degree and eventually became the Vice President of Technology Standards for Sony. "He became an electronics engineer, although there was a brief reunion with Iggy in 1979. But then he retired from music, got an electrical engineering degree, and became the vice president of technology standards for Sony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Jim Morrison's Stage Provocation
xref.body: On October 20, 1967, Iggy Pop attended a Doors concert at the University of Michigan. He was significantly inspired by Jim Morrison's drunken state and the way he provoked the audience, influencing Iggy's own developing stage persona. "Iggy was there and he was inspired by Jim Morrison's drunkenness in the way he provoked the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Later Encouragement for Blah Blah Blah
xref.body: In 1985, Bowie again came to Iggy Pop's aid by listening to rough tapes of new songs and encouraging Iggy and Steve Jones to make another album, leading to "Blah Blah Blah." "In 1985, it was Bowie to the Rescue again. After listening to some rough tapes of some new songs, he encouraged Iggy and his new buddy, ex-sex pistol guitar Steve Jones, to make another album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Mick Jones Inspired by Iggy Pop
xref.body: A young Mick Jones, who would later form The Clash, was present at Iggy Pop's first show outside of the US on July 15, 1972, and was inspired by the performance. "At that gig was a 16-year-old Johnny Liden. So was a young Mick Jones who would later go on to form the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

xref.title: Most Important Post-Garage Rock Band
xref.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were retrospectively identified as the most important of the post-Garage Rock bands. Known for being "drugged out, whacked out, and totally crazy," they were one of the few groups that continued to appeal to audiences after the original Garage Rock sound was thought to be "done" by the late 1960s, and they served as a key inspiration for the first Garage Rock revival (punk). "But in retrospect, the most important of the post garage rock bands, was Iggy Pop and the Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Motor City Ancestor
xref.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges are cited as "Motor City ancestors" who influenced the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, especially inspiring bands like The White Stripes and Yeah Yeah Yeahs. "From there, they ingratiated themselves into the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, all of whom had something in common with motor city ancestors like the Stooges and the MC5."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Move to Berlin - Cold War Artistic Hub
xref.body: In an effort to escape the negative influences surrounding him in L.A. and kick his cocaine addiction, Bowie and Iggy Pop moved to Berlin, Germany. During the height of the Cold War, Berlin was a divided city, yet its unique artistic and bohemian culture provided the perfect environment for Bowie's musical evolution, where he immersed himself in German electronic and crude rock sounds. "He and Iggy Pop packed up and left for Berlin. Now Berlin. Nobody went to Berlin. This was the height of the Cold War."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 2

xref.title: Move to West Berlin with Iggy Pop
xref.body: Deeply influenced by German electronic groups like Kraftwerk, Can, and Neu!, and envisioning electronic music as the future, Bowie moved to West Berlin with Iggy Pop to immerse themselves in the local scene and simultaneously recover from their addictions. They settled in a modest place at Hopstresser 155 in the Schöneberg area, motivated by a belief that remaining in Los Angeles would lead to their demise. "He began to think that these electronic methods of producing music were the future. And what better way to follow this muse than to move to where it all seemed to be happening? Germany."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2

xref.title: Name Change to The Stooges
xref.body: Shortly after their debut as Iggy and the Psychedelic Stooges, the band's name was shortened to simply "The Stooges," marking the beginning of the legend of Iggy Pop. "The psychedelic studios soon became just the stooages. And here begins the legend of Iggy Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Nihilistic Parallel with The Stooges
xref.body: The Velvet Underground are noted for being as nihilistic as Iggy Pop and The Stooges, establishing a parallel in their challenging and dark artistic approach. "They were every bit as nihilistic as the Velvet Underground and violent to boot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Otto Mueller Painting Influence
xref.body: David Bowie was inspired by a painting titled "Lovers Between Garden Walls" by Otto Mueller. He and Iggy Pop encountered this artwork in a Berlin museum around the time *Heroes* was being recorded, adding another layer of artistic influence to the song's lyrical themes. "Bowie and his buddy Iggy Pop saw in a Berlin museum around this time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stories Behind Songs - 5

xref.title: Patronage of Iggy Pop and The Stooges
xref.body: Bowie was a great admirer and musical hero of Iggy Pop, fascinated by his craziness, almost constant mental instability, and ability to see beyond the drugs and self-destructive stage antics to Iggy's intelligence. Bowie convinced his manager to take on Iggy and The Stooges as a project, providing a cash injection that funded their *Raw Power* album. He later visited Iggy when he was in a mental hospital. Bowie's acceptance of Iggy also helped propel the first three Stooges albums to become important templates for punk rock. "Iggy's craziness had made him into one of Bowie's musical heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

xref.title: Pioneers of Punk and Alternative Rock
xref.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were "absolutely bloody essential" in laying the groundwork for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock music that emerged in subsequent decades, suggesting that the landscape of music would be vastly different without their influence. "Iggy Pop and the Stooges were absolutely bloody essential in setting the stage for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock that was to come in the decades ahead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Popularizer of the "Bo Diddley Beat"
xref.body: Bo Diddley is renowned for using a particular rhythm so effectively that it became known as the "Bo Diddley beat." Although the beat itself originated at least 50 years before his time, he was instrumental in introducing it to rock and roll, influencing numerous artists from Iggy Pop to Joan Jett. "Bow didn't invent that beat. It's history goes back at least 50 years, but he was the one who introduced it to rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

xref.title: Possible Shared Recording with Iggy Pop
xref.body: Legend suggests that Billy Joel may have played piano on the Shangri-La's song "Leader of the Pack" on the same record that Iggy Pop allegedly played drums. However, they were never in the studio together; Iggy was paid and sent home before Billy Joel recorded his part. "It's very possible that Iggy Pop played on the same record as Billy Joel."

xref.title: Post-Gorilla Incident Demise
xref.body: Following the bizarre incident with Elton John in the gorilla suit, the mutual admiration between Elton and The Stooges did not lead to a record deal, and the band spiraled towards a breakup, with Iggy Pop deepening his drug use. "Alas, the mutual admiration didn't amount to anything after that. Iggy and the Stooges spiraled towards a breakup, Iggy got deeper into drugs, and Elton never did sign him or the band to a record contract."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1

xref.title: Post-Kyuss Musical Influences
xref.body: Following the breakup of Kyuss, Homme's musical direction was significantly influenced by his discovery of albums like Iggy Pop's "Lust for Life" and "The Idiot," steering him towards a new sound distinct from Kyuss's. "It was around this time that Josh discovered albums like Lust for Life and the Idiot. That was the kind of music he wanted to make now, not whatever Kaya's was doing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Secrets of Queens of the Stone Age: Part 1

xref.title: Prolific Output in the 70s/80s
xref.body: From "Hunky Dory" onward, Bowie released 11 studio albums and two live albums in just over eight and a half years. During this intense period, he also collaborated with artists like Iggy Pop, survived a deep cocaine addiction, and expanded his artistic endeavors into film and theater, taking on projects that regular rock stars typically avoided. "I mean, after all, if we take Hunky Dory as the first album where Bowie got his groove, he had released 11 studio albums in just over 8 and a half years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 2

xref.title: Relocation to Berlin with Iggy Pop
xref.body: After Iggy Pop's hospitalization, David Bowie and Iggy moved to Berlin, where they both cleaned up their drug habits and successfully restarted their respective careers. "Iggy and Bowie moved to Berlin, cleaned up and restarted their careers."

xref.title: Reunion Overtures and Iggy's Reluctance
xref.body: For decades after their initial breakup, various attempts were made to reunite Iggy Pop and the Ashton brothers, but Iggy, whose solo career was flourishing and increasingly drug-free, felt revisiting the past would not be in his best interests. "But things were going so well for Iggy that he just felt that it wouldn't be in his best interests to revisit the past."

xref.title: Rivalry with David Bowie
xref.body: In the early 1970s, Elton John was in a friendly competition with his friend David Bowie over who could be the biggest British rock star. Bowie was also friends with Iggy Pop and working with The Stooges, influencing Elton's desire to prank Bowie and potentially sign The Stooges. "At the time, Elton was in competition with his friend David Bowie over who could be the biggest British rock star."

xref.title: Sampling Nightclubbing
xref.body: In 1994, Trent Reznor sampled the opening beats of Iggy Pop's "Nightclubbing" from "The Idiot." He loaded the beats into a Macintosh computer, inverted the waveform, and added effects to create a new sound, demonstrating innovative use of existing material. "In 1994, Trent Rezner took those beats, loaded them into a Macintosh computer, turned the wave form upside down, added a few extra effects, and got this."

xref.title: Savior of Iggy Pop's Career
xref.body: Bowie visited Iggy Pop in a psychiatric hospital when no one else cared, convincing him not to kill himself and subsequently securing him a new management deal and record contract. This intervention was crucial for Iggy's professional and personal survival. "Bowie was the only person in the world who cared about what happened to Iggy Pop and it was him who finally convinced Iggy that he didn't need to kill himself."

xref.title: Savior of The Stooges
xref.body: Leveraging his influence and industry power, David Bowie convinced Iggy Pop and the Ashton brothers, along with James Williamson, to move to England to record the *Raw Power* album for Columbia Records, effectively restarting The Stooges' career. "Bowie, although not in the greatest shape himself when it came to drugs, turned out to be Iggy's and ultimately the studio's savior."

xref.title: School Dislike and Early Drug Use
xref.body: Despite his intellectual interests, Ian hated school, preferring to stay home with his books and records by Iggy Pop, The Doors, David Bowie, and Lou Reed rather than attend class. Obligatory visits to local retirement homes with classmates were depressing but also led to rifling through medicine cabinets for medication. "Ian hated school. He would rather stay home with his books and Iggy Pop and Doors and David Bowie and Lou Reed records than go to class."

xref.title: Son of Bowie's Costume Designer
xref.body: Saul Hudson, later known as Slash, was the nine-year-old son of Ola Hudson, David Bowie's costume designer. Ola Hudson visited Iggy Pop during his hospitalization in 1974, bringing her son with her. "She had a nine-year-old son named Saul. Saul Hudson. We'd later call him Slash."

xref.title: Soviet Blacklist - Violence
xref.body: This band was listed on the USSR's 1985 "not recommended music" list due to associations with "Violence," with the possibility that the Soviet authorities mistakenly referred to Iggy Pop and The Stooges. Their inclusion reflects the Soviet Union's concerns about the perceived aggressive or disruptive nature of certain Western rock acts. "The Stages, I think they meant Iggy Pop and the Stooges, Violence, ACDC, Neo-Fascism and Violence."

xref.title: Suicide by Hanging
xref.body: After a tumultuous period marked by a collapsing marriage, his mistress's demands, and severe anxiety about the upcoming North American tour, Ian spent the night of May 17, 1980, alone at 77 Barton Street. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, wrote a long note to Deborah with pictures of his wife and baby daughter nearby, then put on Iggy Pop's "The Idiot," and, as the sun rose on Sunday, May 18th, he took a length of rope from the clothesline and hanged himself at the age of 23, discovered by Deborah hours later. "Then he went out into the garden and got himself a length of rope from the clothesline. And as the sun came up and he sang, Ian hanged himself."
